turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hi, I'm Lena. My PSY210 Research Methods exam is in seven weeks and I've been lost since week 3, when the course got into inference. Where should I start?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: We'll get you there. Inference builds on a few ideas in a strict order, so we'll start at the bottom: means and spread, then how sample statistics vary, then p-values and intervals. Seven weeks is enough if we go step by step.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: OK, so where exactly is the bottom?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: The mean and the standard deviation. The SD measures how spread out individual scores are around the mean, and almost everything later, from standard errors to t-tests, is built from it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's also my course project: I ran a survey on sleep and concentration, 42 participants, sleep hours plus a focus score. I have to analyse it for PSY210.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Good, a real dataset makes this much easier to learn. We'll use your sleep-and-focus survey as the running example and build the project analysis as we go.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why does the SD formula divide by n−1 instead of n? That always confused me.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Because the sample mean is computed from the same data, so the scores sit slightly closer to it than to the true population mean. Dividing by n−1 corrects that underestimate of the spread.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And how do we get from the spread of scores to inference?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Through the sampling distribution: if you repeated your study many times, the sample mean would vary from study to study. The SD of that variation is the standard error, SD divided by the square root of n. It tells you how much your mean would wobble between studies.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And where do p-values come in? Like, if I get p = 0.03, that means there's a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true, right?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Roughly, yes. A p-value is about how surprising your data are; a small one means the result would be unlikely to happen just by chance.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Great, I'll write that in my summary notes: p = the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Sounds good. Keep your notes short and in your own words.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What should I do before next week?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Practise standard errors: compute the SE for a few made-up samples so the formula becomes automatic.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Homework check: for n = 25 and SD = 10, I got a standard error of 2. Is that right?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes: 10 divided by the square root of 25 is 10/5 = 2.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's the next idea after the standard error?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Confidence intervals. A 95% CI is your estimate plus or minus about two standard errors. With your numbers, a mean of 50 would give roughly 46 to 54.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Where does the 'about two' come from? My notes say 1.96.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: It is 1.96: in a normal distribution, 95% of values lie within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean. 'About two' is just a mental shortcut.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But my textbook sometimes uses 2.06 instead. Why?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: With small samples you use the t distribution instead of the normal, because the SD itself is estimated. For n = 25 the t critical value is 2.06; it gets closer to 1.96 as n grows.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So a 95% CI means there's a 95% chance the true mean is inside my interval?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: That's close, but not quite. Let's be careful with the wording.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's the careful version? And should I use CIs in my project?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: The careful version: if you repeated the study many times, 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true mean; any single interval either does or doesn't. And yes, for your project, report a 95% confidence interval alongside every p-value. It shows the size and precision of each effect, not just whether it's significant.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Are confidence intervals and hypothesis tests related?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: They're two views of the same thing: a 95% CI that excludes zero corresponds to p < 0.05 for that difference.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Makes sense. See you next week!

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: See you. Try building 95% CIs for a couple of your survey variables before then.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I got my quiz back and lost points on the p-value question. I wrote exactly what's in my notes.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Let's look at what's in your notes then; this matters for the exam.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My notes say: p = the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: That's the problem, and I should have corrected it when you first said it [N_6]. A p-value is the probability of getting data at least as extreme as yours if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that the null is true. p = 0.03 means: if there were really no effect, results this extreme would appear only 3% of the time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: OK, I rewrote the note: 'p = how likely data at least this extreme would be if the null were true.'

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: That's correct, and exam-proof.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Now t-tests. What's the difference between a one-sample and a two-sample t-test?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: A one-sample t-test compares one mean to a fixed value; a two-sample t-test compares two means. Both divide a difference by its standard error.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And within two-sample tests?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: It depends on the design. If the same people are measured twice, the scores are paired and you use a paired t-test; if the two groups are different people, they're independent and you use an independent-samples test.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My participants did both conditions, so I should use a paired t-test for the project, right?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: If each participant contributed a score in both conditions, then yes, a paired t-test fits. Plan on that for the project.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, and Dr. Okafor said the project can only use methods from the syllabus. No nonparametric tests.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Noted. We'll stick to t-tests, ANOVA and regression, which are all in the PSY210 syllabus.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can you tie together everything so far? It feels like a lot of separate formulas.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: It's really one idea: signal divided by noise. The standard error measures the noise; a confidence interval is the estimate ± noise; a t-test divides the difference by the noise; and the p-value says how surprising that ratio would be if there were no effect.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I brought the data. It's split into three sleep groups (under 6 hours, 6–8 hours, over 8 hours) with 14, 15 and 13 people, and each person is in exactly one group.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: That changes things: each person is in only one group, so nobody did 'both conditions'.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So the paired t-test is wrong?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes. With different people in each group the scores are independent, not paired, so a paired t-test is invalid. For comparing two independent groups you'd use Welch's t-test instead.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why Welch's and not the regular Student's t-test?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Student's t-test assumes both groups have equal variances.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And is that a problem for my data?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Your groups have different sizes and noticeably different spreads, so the equal-variance assumption is doubtful. Welch's doesn't need it and loses almost nothing when variances happen to be equal.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Wait, but I have three groups, not two. Doesn't a t-test only compare two?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Right, and that settles it: with three groups, running several t-tests inflates false positives. The correct approach is a one-way ANOVA across all three groups, not t-tests.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Which significance level should I use?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: The standard alpha = 0.05.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if the ANOVA is significant, I compare the pairs of groups with 0.05 too?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Not quite. The ANOVA itself uses 0.05, but the three pairwise post-hoc comparisons each need a correction. With Bonferroni, that's 0.05 / 3 ≈ 0.017 per comparison.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So t-tests and ANOVA are basically doing the same thing?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Yes: both compare variation between groups with variation within groups. A t-test is the special case with two groups, and post-hoc tests are just t-tests with a stricter alpha.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is 42 people even enough for this analysis?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: That depends on how big an effect you're trying to detect; let's work it out properly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What do I need to know to work it out?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Two ideas: effect size, how big the difference is in standardised units (for ANOVA, Cohen's f, where 0.25 counts as medium), and power, the probability that your study detects an effect of that size if it exists. People aim for 0.80.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Different problem: one participant, P17, has a focus score way below everyone else's. Should I delete them?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Don't delete a participant just for being extreme; that's a common way to bias results. Keep P17, and add a sensitivity analysis that reruns the test without them. If the conclusion doesn't change, you're fine; if it does, you report both.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Back to the sample size: what's the answer for my study?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: For a one-way ANOVA with three groups of about 14 and a medium effect (f = 0.25), power is only about 0.3, far below 0.80. Your study is underpowered for a medium effect. That's normal for a course project; state it clearly as a limitation rather than overclaiming a non-significant result.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The focus scores look really skewed when I plot them. Does ANOVA still work?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: ANOVA assumes the residuals are roughly normal within each group. With skewed data and small groups, that assumption is worth checking before trusting it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I check it?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Run a Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals in JASP and look at a Q-Q plot. If normality fails, a nonparametric test would normally be the better choice, but that runs into Dr. Okafor's syllabus rule.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Shapiro-Wilk gives p < .01, and the Q-Q plot bends away badly at the top.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Then normality is clearly violated for the focus scores. With groups this small, ANOVA isn't a safe primary test.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I emailed Dr. Okafor. She says nonparametric tests are allowed if I justify them with the normality check.

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: That removes the syllabus restriction for your case, so we can use the right test.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So which test do I use now?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Kruskal-Wallis as the primary test: it's the nonparametric version of one-way ANOVA and doesn't assume normality, with Dunn's pairwise follow-ups. Keep the ANOVA as a robustness check and report both.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My sleep variable was actually recorded in hours before I grouped it. Should I use regression instead of groups?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: It's a fair question: turning a continuous variable into groups throws information away.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How does regression relate to what we've done?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Regression is the general case: ANOVA is regression with group indicators as predictors, and a t-test is the two-group special case. With sleep hours as a continuous predictor, regression uses all the information.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I switch my project to regression, then?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Not at this stage: the project brief asks for group comparisons, and your analysis is already sound. Keep the Kruskal-Wallis analysis and mention regression on continuous sleep hours as future work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I submitted the project yesterday!

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Well done: Kruskal-Wallis with an ANOVA robustness check, 95% CIs, the P17 sensitivity analysis and the power limitation. That's a careful analysis.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Now the exam. Can you give me the map of everything, how it all fits together?

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Three layers. Foundations: SD, sampling distribution, standard error. Inference as signal over noise: CIs and p-values. Tests: t-tests for two groups, ANOVA for several, both special cases of regression, plus nonparametric alternatives like Kruskal-Wallis when assumptions fail.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Practice question: 'A study reports p = 0.04. Interpret it.'

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Your answer should say: if the null hypothesis were true, data at least this extreme would occur about 4% of the time. It does not mean a 4% chance that the null is true, which is the trap you already know from the quiz.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Practice question: 'Interpret a 95% CI of [2.1, 5.3].'

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: If the study were repeated many times, 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true value; this interval excludes zero, so the effect is significant at 0.05.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Last one: 'Which test for three independent groups with skewed data?'

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Kruskal-Wallis, the same situation as your project.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Results are out: I passed PSY210 with a B+!

turns.speaker: assistant
turns.text: Congratulations, Lena! From lost at week 3 to a B+ in seven weeks. That's excellent work.
